config.title: Dependency security

intro.title: Dependency security
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Node.js application that checks for outdated and vulnerable dependencies in its package.json file. You will learn the core concept of dependency security, which involves managing third-party libraries to prevent security risks. The main technologies involved are npm (Node Package Manager) for dependency management and a security auditing tool like npm audit. By the end, you will understand how to identify and address security vulnerabilities in your project's dependencies.
intro.usecase: Dependency security is crucial in modern web applications where third-party libraries power everything from interactive dashboards to authentication forms. Developers encounter this daily when using npm packages for UI components like modals, data visualization charts, or form validation libraries. A vulnerable dependency in a payment processing form or admin panel could expose sensitive user data or enable injection attacks. Proper dependency management ensures that features like real-time filtering panels, interactive maps, and user profile editors remain secure against known exploits.

objectives: Implement a dependency scanning tool to identify known vulnerabilities
Configure automated dependency updates to maintain security patches
Apply version pinning to control dependency updates and prevent breaking changes
Integrate dependency security checks into a continuous integration pipeline
Manipulate dependency lock files to ensure reproducible builds
Initialize a dependency audit to generate vulnerability reports
Construct a security policy for third-party library usage

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from 'react' to set up the React environment with state management.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have React and useState imported and ready to use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, setting up the foundation for state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the DependencySecurity component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named DependencySecurity that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the DependencySecurity component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A component named DependencySecurity is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The component is named DependencySecurity and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main component structure. This component will later contain our dependency security demonstration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your component is named exactly 'DependencySecurity' and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a component named 'DependencySecurity' that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize state for dependency list
steps.instruction: Inside your DependencySecurity component, use useState to create a state variable named 'dependencies' initialized with an empty array.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] as the initial value, and destructure the returned array into the state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with an empty array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'dependencies' ready to store dependency data.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with [] and destructured into 'dependencies' and 'setDependencies' variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've initialized state to track dependencies. This will allow us to manage and display dependency security information.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with an empty array [] and destructuring the result into two variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Use useState([]) to create a state variable named 'dependencies' and its setter function.

steps.title: Initialize state for vulnerability status
steps.instruction: Inside your DependencySecurity component, use useState to create a state variable named 'hasVulnerabilities' and initialize it to false.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call below your existing state for dependency list. The initial value should be false.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a boolean state variable
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two state variables: one for dependencies and one for tracking whether vulnerabilities exist.
successCriteria: A state variable 'hasVulnerabilities' is declared using useState and initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added state to track vulnerability status. This boolean will help us monitor security risks in our dependencies.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState to create a variable named 'hasVulnerabilities' with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a second useState call inside your component to create a boolean state variable for tracking vulnerabilities.

steps.title: Define function to add dependency
steps.instruction: Inside the DependencySecurity component, create a function named 'addDependency' that takes a dependency object as a parameter and adds it to the dependencies state using setDependencies.
steps.hint: The function should update the state by appending the new dependency to the existing dependencies array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named addDependency is defined that updates the dependencies state by appending a new dependency object.
successCriteria: The addDependency function is defined, takes a parameter, and uses setDependencies to update the state with the new dependency.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the addDependency function. This handler will allow you to manage dependency additions securely.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named addDependency, takes a parameter, and properly updates the dependencies state using setDependencies.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is not defined correctly. Ensure you create a function named addDependency that takes a dependency object and updates the dependencies state.

steps.title: Define function to check for vulnerabilities
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a function named 'checkVulnerabilities' that examines the dependencies array and updates the vulnerability status state.
steps.hint: The function should check if any dependency in the array contains 'vulnerable' in its name and update the state accordingly.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named checkVulnerabilities is defined that will later be used to validate dependency security.
successCriteria: The checkVulnerabilities function is created and includes logic to examine dependencies and update hasVulnerabilities state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the vulnerability checking function. This is essential for dependency security validation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the function, but make sure it properly examines the dependencies array and updates the vulnerability state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Check that you've named it 'checkVulnerabilities' and included the security validation logic.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, replace the current return value with a div element that has the class 'dependency-security' and contains an h1 heading with the text 'Dependency Security Dashboard'.
steps.hint: Remember to return the div element from your component. The heading should be a direct child of the div.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a structured container with a heading, providing the foundation for the dependency security UI.
successCriteria: The component returns a div with class 'dependency-security' containing an h1 heading with the exact text 'Dependency Security Dashboard'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main container structure for your dependency security dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your div has the correct class name and contains the exact heading text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure doesn't match the requirements. Check that you're returning a div with class 'dependency-security' and an h1 heading inside it.

steps.title: Display dependency list
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a section to display the current dependencies. Show each dependency's name and version from the dependencies state array.
steps.hint: You can map over the dependencies array to create list items. Each dependency object should have name and version properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will render a list showing each dependency's name and version when dependencies are added.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a section that maps over the dependencies state array and displays each dependency's name and version properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the dependency list display. This shows how to render dynamic data from state in a security context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some list display code, but make sure you're mapping over the dependencies array and displaying both name and version properties for each item.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dependency list isn't displaying correctly. Check that you're using the dependencies state array and showing both name and version for each dependency.

steps.title: Add vulnerability status display
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph that displays the vulnerability status based on the hasVulnerabilities state. Use a ternary operator to show 'Vulnerabilities detected! Update dependencies.' when hasVulnerabilities is true, and 'No vulnerabilities found.' when false.
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator directly in JSX: {hasVulnerabilities ? 'Warning message' : 'OK message'}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will display a paragraph showing either a vulnerability warning or an all-clear message based on the current state.
successCriteria: A paragraph element exists that uses the hasVulnerabilities state with a ternary operator to display appropriate security status messages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional vulnerability status display. This helps users immediately see security assessment results.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the hasVulnerabilities state variable and a ternary operator to show different messages for true and false states.
steps.feedbackWrong: The vulnerability status display isn't working correctly. Check that you're using the hasVulnerabilities state and a ternary operator to show appropriate messages for both true and false conditions.

steps.title: Add check button and wire to handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside your component's return statement that, when clicked, calls the checkVulnerabilities function to trigger a security assessment.
steps.hint: Use the <button> tag with an onClick attribute that references your checkVulnerabilities function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button to trigger an action
<button onClick={handleClick}>Check Status</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button appears in your component that will trigger the vulnerability check when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element with onClick={checkVulnerabilities} is added to the component's return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that will trigger security checks when clicked, completing the user interaction for dependency security assessment.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but it doesn't yet call the checkVulnerabilities function when clicked. Make sure to add the onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured to trigger the vulnerability check. Remember to add onClick={checkVulnerabilities} to your button element.
